templates.name: Addition/similarity: a further item of the same kind
Contrast: established view or appearance, then a finding that breaks it
Contrast: positive claim, then a limiting fact about the same subject
Cause/effect: condition, principle or evidence, then its consequence
Cause/effect: need or judgment, then the action it motivates
Concession: grant, then the main claim resumes (but / Still)
Purpose and aptness: goal then deliberate act, or a fitting echo
Specification/restatement: exact content or plain rewording
Sequence/time: next step, earlier or later event, end of a long effort
Culmination, alternative and place (ultimately, alternatively, there)
Example: general claim, then one named instance

items.subtype: Concession: grant then turn
items.passage: Mongolian long song is not named for the length of its lyrics. The name refers instead to its prolonged syllables, each sustained across an ornate melodic line. ______ vocalists in numerous traditions extend individual syllables over several notes, but long-song performers carry the practice so far that a performance of several minutes may contain only a few lines of text.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The opening sentences say long song is named for “its prolonged syllables, each sustained across an ornate melodic line.” The blank sentence first grants a point that seems to make this ordinary: “vocalists in numerous traditions extend individual syllables over several notes.” Its “but” clause then returns to what sets long song apart. “Of course” fits, since it introduces a point the writer concedes before making the main claim.

A.why_wrong: The first clause of the blank sentence is about vocalists in many other traditions, so it does not give the exact content of the claim about long song; it concedes a point before the “but” clause.

B.why_wrong: The way long song got its name does not cause vocalists in other traditions to extend syllables; the blank sentence grants a point rather than stating a result.

D.why_wrong: The first clause of the blank sentence is not a further point about long song but a concession about other traditions, which the “but” clause then answers.

items.notes: Grant then turn inside one sentence (3.17 shape: Of course ... but), not the Still shape b1 used. K1 has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/transitions.md section 5), so this is written as a strong band 6 and band_target is 6, not the 7 the plan asked for. No contrast decoy (contrast and concession exclude each other) and no In fact, Indeed or Actually beside the concession key. Trap: Furthermore and Specifically for a reader who takes the blank sentence as more detail about long song. items.subtype: Specification: the more common case (more often)
items.passage: Canvas, now the usual support for paintings, became standard only gradually. In fifteenth-century Europe, painters seldom chose it for altarpieces or portraits, keeping it mainly for processional banners and other works that had to be carried or rolled; ______ they painted altarpieces and portraits on wooden panels—poplar in Italy, oak in Flanders—prepared with smooth layers of gesso.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The clause before the blank says painters “seldom chose it,” meaning canvas, “for altarpieces or portraits.” The clause after it names what they usually did instead: “they painted altarpieces and portraits on wooden panels.” “More often” signals that panels were the more common choice, compared with the rare use of canvas for such works.

A.why_wrong: “Nevertheless” would mean that painters used panels in spite of the preceding point, but the rare use of canvas for these works is exactly why panels were the usual choice; the clauses agree.

C.why_wrong: Panels were not a further practice alongside the rare use of canvas for these works; they were the usual alternative to it, which is a comparison of frequency, not an addition.

D.why_wrong: “That said” would mark the panel clause as a qualification of the preceding claim, but it confirms that claim by naming the more common practice.

items.notes: Band-7 S1 frequency form (spec/rw/band7/transitions.md section 5) on the 4b7a84b0 architecture: no popular-image opener, no study, no researchers-found interrupter (five live S1 items already use that frame); the blank follows a semicolon. Moves: surface contrast (seldom canvas, then panels) with a non-adversative key; a synonym pair of concession decoys (nevertheless, that said) and one additive decoy; key outside the core 13; no sequence or summary decoy. No for this reason or other causal decoy, since a reader could take the panels as the result of canvas being kept for banners. items.subtype: Alternative: a different method for the same task
items.passage: Oceanographers typically chart the seafloor from ships equipped with multibeam sonar, which calculates depth by timing the echoes of sound pulses that bounce off the bottom. ______ the seafloor can be mapped from orbit: satellites measure the height of the sea surface, which bulges slightly above underwater mountains because their mass pulls extra water toward them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes one way of mapping the seafloor: from ships “equipped with multibeam sonar.” The blank sentence describes a different way of doing the same job: “the seafloor can be mapped from orbit” by satellites that measure “the height of the sea surface.” “Alternatively” fits, since it introduces a second, different method for the same task.

B.why_wrong: Mapping from orbit is not an instance of mapping with ships and sonar; it is a separate method.

C.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not reword the description of sonar mapping; it describes a different technique that relies on satellites and the height of the sea surface.

D.why_wrong: Ships using sonar do not lead to mapping from orbit; the sentences describe two independent methods.

items.notes: Alternative method (3.16 shape), band 6 by plan. No instead, by contrast or however among the options (each could link two methods), and the first sentence states no limitation of sonar, so no causal decoy can read as defensible. Ultimately is already the key of seven live U1 items, so this one keys Alternatively. items.subtype: Consequence: a misconception that looks like a contrast
items.passage: Club mosses are evergreen plants common on temperate woodland floors. Their creeping stems, densely clothed in tiny, overlapping leaves, give colonies the appearance of a plush green carpet. ______ these plants are often mistaken for true mosses, when in fact they are vascular plants, possessing internal tissues that transport water and nutrients, and are more closely related to ferns than to mosses.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The text describes how club mosses look: their stems, “densely clothed in tiny, overlapping leaves, give colonies the appearance of a plush green carpet.” That mosslike look leads to the belief the blank sentence reports: “these plants are often mistaken for true mosses.” The words “when in fact” correct that belief, not the earlier sentences. “Hence” fits, since it introduces a consequence of the plants’ appearance.

A.why_wrong: The words “when in fact” make the blank sentence look like a reversal, but what they correct is the common belief, not the description before the blank. The belief that club mosses are true mosses follows from their carpetlike look; it does not contrast with it.

B.why_wrong: The common belief about club mosses is not one example of their creeping stems and tiny leaves; it is a result of how those features make the plants look.

C.why_wrong: “That said” would mark the blank sentence as a qualification of the description of the plants, but it does not limit that description; it reports a belief that the plants’ appearance produces.

items.subtype: Contrast: two instruments, opposite bowing
items.passage: Violinists position the bow outside the instrument’s strings, drawing its horsehair across them from above. On the erhu, a two-stringed Chinese fiddle, ______ the horsehair is permanently threaded between the strings, and performers sound either string by pressing the hair against it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says violinists position the bow “outside the instrument’s strings.” The blank sentence says that on the erhu “the horsehair is permanently threaded between the strings.” These are two instruments bowed in opposite ways, so “by contrast” fits.

A.why_wrong: The erhu is not an example of the violin’s way of bowing; it works in the opposite way.

C.why_wrong: How violinists position the bow does not cause the erhu’s horsehair to pass between its strings; the sentences describe two different instruments.

D.why_wrong: “Similarly” would say the erhu is bowed the way a violin is, but its horsehair runs between the strings rather than across them from outside.

items.subtype: Contrast: two groups of animals, opposite behavior
items.passage: Most living turtle species retract the head by withdrawing it straight backward into the shell, compressing the neck into a vertical S-shaped curve. Side-necked turtles, distributed across South America, Africa, and Australia, ______ bend the neck horizontally, tucking the head beneath the overhanging forward edge of the upper shell.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says most turtle species retract the head “by withdrawing it straight backward into the shell.” The blank sentence says side-necked turtles “bend the neck horizontally.” The two groups withdraw the head in opposite ways, so “in contrast” fits.

A.why_wrong: Side-necked turtles are turtles, but they are not an example of withdrawing the head straight backward; they are the group that bends the neck sideways.

B.why_wrong: The way most turtles retract the head does not cause side-necked turtles to bend the neck sideways.

C.why_wrong: “Likewise” would say side-necked turtles withdraw the head the same way, but they bend the neck horizontally rather than withdrawing the head straight backward.

items.subtype: Addition: a second contribution by the same person
items.passage: Japanese origami artist Akira Yoshizawa pioneered wet-folding, a technique in which the paper is slightly dampened so that it can be sculpted into rounded, naturalistic forms rather than only angular ones. ______ he devised a standardized notation of dashed lines, dotted lines, and arrows, enabling enthusiasts to reproduce models from printed diagrams.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes one of Yoshizawa’s contributions: he “pioneered wet-folding.” The blank sentence describes a second, separate one: he “devised a standardized notation of dashed lines, dotted lines, and arrows.” “Additionally” fits, since it adds a further achievement of the same kind.

B.why_wrong: The notation is not a rewording of wet-folding; it is a different contribution.

C.why_wrong: “Instead” would mean Yoshizawa devised the notation in place of pioneering wet-folding, but he did both.

D.why_wrong: Pioneering wet-folding did not lead to the notation; the two are independent contributions.

items.subtype: Specification: the exact rule behind a general statement
items.passage: Turkish exhibits vowel harmony. Under this phonological principle, the vowels of suffixes attached to a word systematically adjust to resemble the vowels of the root. ______ a suffix contains a front vowel, articulated toward the front of the mouth, whenever the root’s final vowel is also a front vowel, and a back vowel whenever that final vowel is articulated farther back.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence states the general principle: the vowels of suffixes “systematically adjust to resemble the vowels of the root.” The blank sentence gives its exact content, saying which kind of vowel a suffix takes depending on “the root’s final vowel.” “Specifically” fits, since it introduces a more precise version of the previous statement.

A.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not offer an opposing point; it spells out the principle. Its contrast between front and back vowels lies inside the sentence, not between the sentences.

B.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not add a separate fact about Turkish; it explains precisely how the adjustment described in the previous sentence works.

D.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not describe a similar case; it describes the same principle in more detail.

items.notes: General statement, then its exact content (2.12 shape), keyed Specifically. No example decoy (example and specification exclude each other) and no causal decoy. items.subtype: Restatement: a term, then its plain meaning

B.why_wrong: “Borrowed scenery” is not something gardens incorporate in addition to shakkei; it is what shakkei means.

C.why_wrong: Nothing after the blank works against the statement that gardens incorporate shakkei; the words explain it.

items.subtype: Contrast: a hypothesis, then the finding that overturned it
items.passage: In the 1840s, British naturalist Edward Forbes, recovering progressively fewer organisms in his dredges as he sampled deeper waters, proposed that no life existed in the ocean below approximately 550 meters. ______ in the decades that followed, deep-sea expeditions retrieved starfish, sponges, and numerous other animals from depths of several thousand meters.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: Forbes “proposed that no life existed in the ocean below approximately 550 meters.” The blank sentence reports finds that contradict that idea: expeditions “retrieved starfish, sponges, and numerous other animals from depths of several thousand meters.” “However” fits, since it introduces a finding that contrasts with the earlier view.

B.why_wrong: The deep-sea finds are not an instance of Forbes’s proposal; they show that it was wrong.

C.why_wrong: “Similarly” would say the expeditions supported the same conclusion, but finding animals thousands of meters down contradicts the claim that no life existed below about 550 meters.

D.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not reword Forbes’s proposal; it reports later evidence against it.

items.notes: Established view, then a finding that breaks it, keyed However (2.1 relation, sentence-initial as in 1.1). No causal decoy: a reader could argue that Forbes’s claim prompted the later expeditions. Forbes’s azoic hypothesis (about 300 fathoms) is described as he stated it; no expedition or later researcher is named. items.subtype: Consequence: a physical property, then its effect
items.passage: In the ocean, sound travels most slowly within a layer roughly a kilometer down. Sound waves straying above or below this layer are refracted back into it, so the layer functions as a channel that keeps sound from dispersing. ______ low-frequency sounds generated within the channel, including certain whale vocalizations, can be detected thousands of kilometers away.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence explains that the slow-sound layer “functions as a channel that keeps sound from dispersing.” Because sound in the channel does not spread out and fade, sounds made there can travel very far: they “can be detected thousands of kilometers away.” “Hence” fits, since it introduces a consequence of the previous point.

A.why_wrong: “Nevertheless” would mean the sounds travel far in spite of the channel, but they travel far because of it.

C.why_wrong: The blank sentence is not a similar, separate fact; it is what follows from the channel keeping sound from dispersing.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text places the long-distance detection of sounds before the description of the channel; it is a result of the channel.

items.notes: Property, then consequence, keyed Hence (2.14 key). No example decoy: whale calls could otherwise be read as an instance of sound carried by the channel. The layer’s depth is given loosely (it varies with latitude). Transitions: no web check (WAVE.md, 2026-10-16); real subject described from general knowledge, no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.subtype: Consequence: a law, then a result of it
items.passage: In 2008, Ecuador adopted a constitution that grants nature legal rights, including the right to exist and regenerate, and allows any citizen to defend those rights in court. ______ in 2011, two residents successfully sued a provincial government on behalf of the Vilcabamba River, which road construction had been filling with debris.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says Ecuador’s 2008 constitution “allows any citizen to defend those rights in court.” The blank sentence describes what followed from that: in 2011, two residents “successfully sued a provincial government on behalf of the Vilcabamba River.” “As a result” fits, since the lawsuit was possible because of the constitution.

A.why_wrong: The lawsuit is not a similar, separate development; it was made possible by the constitution.

B.why_wrong: “Nevertheless” would mean the lawsuit succeeded in spite of the constitution, but the constitution is what allowed it.
